proposals.relationship: Kealey adopts Thompson’s focus on class as developing behavior and defends the materiality of culture while requiring that British insights be tested in Canada.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1981: 85–87 explicitly stands with Thompson and Raymond Williams on culture, then distinguishes objective class parameters from Thompson’s terrain of changing behavior and class-for-itself. He concedes some cultural work neglects economy and that imported methods require contextual demonstration. This is his specific methodological resource, beyond the existing broader field route 890, not wholesale agreement or a fresh reading of the complete Thompson originals. Williams and Hobsbawm retain distinct roles.

proposals.relationship: Kealey uses Raymond Williams’s account of culture and revisable hegemony to explain both working-class resistance and its limits.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1981: 80/n 30–31 uses Keywords and Politics and Letters to frame culture as activity and a whole way of life; 85/n 42 defends its materiality. At 89/n 59 and 90/n 61, Williams supplies the distinctions between class conflict and class struggle and the account of continuously renewed, resisted hegemony. Gramsci is explicitly mediated through Williams, and separate Eley–Nield discussion is credited. Culture does not require universal solidarity or perpetual militancy; defeat needs explanation. These are Raymond’s works, not Eric Williams or every cited Williams; originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Kealey uses Hobsbawm’s account of artisans’ respectability and class consciousness when interpreting skilled Canadian workers’ institutions and politics.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1981: 85/n 45 invokes Hobsbawm on the objective side of class. At 87/n 50 he uses The Aristocracy of Labour Reconsidered to reject the equation of respectability with simple embourgeoisement, then connects the findings to Hamilton and Toronto research 87–88. The labour-aristocracy literature is plural and contested; the cited Canadian studies and worker agency retain distinct credit. This is specific use, not proof that every British model fits Canada or a fresh reading of the cited originals.

proposals.relationship: Kealey invokes Tilly’s aspiration to overcome disciplinary division between history and sociology as a stated aim of his edited collection.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 introduction 5 explicitly quotes Tilly’s 1981 aspiration and presents the volume as pursuing it. His opening 1 describes the editorial project, and 5 insists on empirical research while acknowledging methodological differences. This is a particular editorial and methodological resource, not formal supervision, adoption of all Tilly’s collective-action models, or credit for every contributor’s article. Tilly and Michael Katz’s shared quantitative-project role on 4 remains distinct; original Tilly book unread.
primary_locators: 1988 introduction 1 and 5; Tilly 1981/1984 references 7; actual publisher PDF web text

proposals.relationship: Kealey explicitly says that confronting McKay’s materialist critique of Thompson and culturalism benefited his thinking.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1981: 91/n 63 calls the unpublished 1980 Towards a Materialist Approach to Canadian Labour History a particularly substantive critique and explicitly acknowledges benefit from confronting it. This is direct Kealey testimony about the critical resource; the unpublished text itself is unread. It is distinct from the later published 1981–82 Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture, whose complete original remains unread this turn; neither agreement with every objection nor identity of versions is assumed. McKay also receives draft-comment credit 94.

proposals.relationship: Kealey uses Stedman Jones’s discussion of history and the social sciences to insist on critical, historically informed borrowing of methods.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1981: 86/n 46 calls From Historical Sociology to Theoretical History the best discussion he knows of the problem of borrowing concepts without understanding disciplinary debates. The same note calls Class Expression Versus Social Control a specific critique of unreflective borrowing; 91/n 64 returns to the former. Thompson and the opposed defense of social control by Moorhouse retain distinct credit. This is a particular methodological resource, not agreement with Stedman Jones’s later language-of-class arguments or a new reading of those original articles.

proposals.relationship: Kealey calls Cook’s worry that a golden age of Canadian historical writing was ending premature, arguing that working-class studies could transform the historical synthesis.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1978: 116/n 1–2 identifies Cook’s limited-identities call and Golden Age essay. At 135 he calls the earlier pluralism refreshing and liberating while disputing analytical separation of class, ethnicity and place, then explicitly labels Cook’s pessimistic forecast premature. The criticism retains the acknowledged achievement and does not undo Cook’s distinct teaching influence 2694 or claim all Cook scholarship rejects labour history. Original Cook 1967/1977 texts not newly read.
primary_locators: 1978 printed 116–117/n 1–9 and 134–135, especially final signed paragraph 135; actual 135 visually checked

proposals.relationship: Kealey criticizes Berger’s handling of the new history for confusing critical inquiry with a mission to provide a positive national account.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1988 introduction 2 quotes Berger’s 1986 conclusion 320 and immediately charges confusion between critical scholarship and national mythology. He introduces Berger as even-handed before criticizing this aspect, then compares Careless’s changing position 2–3, already 998. This records Kealey’s reading of the quoted passage, not an independently established summary of the entire unread Berger book. The later 1995 quoted acknowledgment of finding little to contest in Berger’s labour-history summary, already group 941, is preserved.
